name: Fròʔò, a dialect of Tagbana
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Traoré, Yranahan & Caroline Féry. 2019. Syllable structure and loanword adaptation in Fròʔò. In Samson Lotven, Silvina Bongiovanni, Phillip Weirich, Robert Botne & Samuel Gyasi Obeng (eds.), African linguistics across the disciplines: Selected papers from the 48th Annual Conference on African Linguistics, 1–28. Berlin: Language Science Press. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.3520565 (open access)
catalog_locator: p. 13, §3.1 'Vowel deletion leading to CVC syllables' (of the saved chapter PDF; fn. 5 same page); tone statement p. 3, §1.
catalog_quote: [p. 13, §3.1] If some conditions are met, when two morphemes come together, the last vowel of the first morpheme or word deletes, and a coda is created. We refrain from calling the process “vowel syncope”, since that would imply that it is an unstressed vowel that is deleted. However, there is no evidence whatever for stress in Fròʔò. Vowel deletion in Fròʔò touches all vowels equally.[fn. 5: High vowels are not deleted more easily than mid or low vowels, as is the case in the neighboring Bamana, Colloquial Bambara (see Green et al. 2014).] [p. 3, §1] Fròʔò has three level tones, high (H), mid (M) and low (L). There are no contour tones. The syllable is the tone bearing unit (TBU) and every syllable in every word carries its own tone, regardless of the category and the length of the word. In other words, all vowels in the language bear one of these three tones.
world_status: statement found in an open source

Printed p.13, §3.1 'Vowel deletion leading to CVC syllables' reads exactly: 'If some conditions are met, when two morphemes come together, the last vowel of the first morpheme or word deletes, and a coda is created. The second (tone) part of the quote is a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Fròʔò (Tagbana) is described as a three-level tone language in which every syllable bears its own tone; the authors (one a native-speaker linguist) state there is no evidence at all for word stress, and vowel deletion is not conditioned by any stressed/unstressed distinction.
new_statements.exceptions: None in this source. Note a later exploratory proposal by the same first author (Traore 2024, IJAMRS 4(1): 1053) that certain nouns carry an underlying lexical 'quantitative accent' manifesting as vowel lengthening before [l]; it gives no placement rule and does not claim general word stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the word-level phonology of the Fròʔò dialect (Fronan); made in passing while motivating terminology for a vowel-deletion process, not in a dedicated prosody section. Tone (H/M/L + floating tones) is the described word-prosodic system (Rialland, Traoré & Féry 2021).
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe the Fròʔò dialect of Tagbana, spoken around Fronan (the second author's native variety); Glottolog tagw1240 'Tagwana Senoufo' [tgw] covers Tagbana as a whole (other dialects: Takper of Niakaramandougou described by Hérault & Mlanhoro 1973, Katiola dialect in Bothel's mss.). No separate glottocode for Fròʔò is known to me.

new_statements.quote: [p. 52, §4.4.1 'Feststellung der Töne':] Anhand des uns zur Verfügung stehenden Korpus haben wir im Tagbana 3 Töne feststellen können. Diese Feststellung stimmt mit der von Mensah und Tchagbalé (1983, 53) überein. Demnach seien die 3 Töne im Tagbana die folgenden: hoch [´] mitte (unbezeichnet) tief [`] [p. 105, §6.2.1, list of the information a lexical entry must carry:] phonologische Informationen - phonologischer Aufbau des Wortes - Wortakzent, wobei wir im Hinblick auf unser Wörterbuch von Tonmuster sprechen werden
new_statements.translation: [p. 52:] On the basis of the corpus available to us we were able to establish 3 tones in Tagbana. This finding agrees with that of Mensah and Tchagbalé (1983, 53). Accordingly the 3 tones of Tagbana are: high [´], mid (unmarked), low [`]. [p. 105:] phonological information - phonological make-up of the word - word accent, in place of which, for our dictionary, we shall speak of tone pattern.

new_statements.relation_note: Consistent with the catalog's no-word-stress record (Traoré & Féry 2019: 13): Katia Kamara 1988 treats Tagbana as a three-tone language, marks only tone, and replaces 'word accent' by 'tone pattern' as the prosodic information of a lexical entry (p. 105); it adds the three-tone inventory and tone-lowering rules for the Katiola dialect (Traoré & Féry likewise give H, M, L for Fròʔò). It does not contain an explicit sentence denying stress, so the explicit no-stress statement of record remains Traoré & Féry 2019; nothing here contradicts it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tagbana (Katiola dialect) is described as a tone language with three level tones (high, mid unmarked, low; the mid tone provisionally derived from H/L by lowering rules T->M/_H, H->M/H_, H->M/_T, so that disyllables never surface as HT or TH). No word stress or accent is marked or discussed anywhere in the phonology chapter or the 280-page lexicon; where a lexical entry would carry 'Wortakzent' the author explicitly substitutes the word's tone pattern. The work never states in so many words that stress is absent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned (no stress of any kind is marked)
new_statements.exceptions: none. Note: the labels 'betont/unbetont' in §5.3.1 Personalpronomen (pp. 57-58) denote the emphatic vs. plain pronoun series (French tonique/atone), not word stress: 'Die betonten Subjektpersonalpronomen sowie die betonten und unbetonten Objektpersonalpronomina haben Mittelton' (p. 58); likewise '(Betonung)' in the interlinear glosses of the texts marks an emphatic pronoun.
new_statements.identity_note: Katia Kamara 1988 describes the Tagbana of Katiola town (the author's own variety; §2.2 p. 10 explicitly distinguishes it from takpɛrɛ, the speech of Niakaramandougou described by Clamens 1952 and Böthel 1966 via Delafosse's informant). The catalog record and Traoré & Féry's papers describe Fròʔò, the Tagbana dialect of Fronan. Both are dialects of Tagwana Senoufo (tagw1240).

tone_statements.citation: Coulibaly, Mamadou Gninnatcha Eugène. 2023. Paramètres prosodiques des tons de la langue tagbana. Ziglôbitha, Revue des Arts, Linguistique, Littérature & Civilisations 2(8) (décembre 2023): 5–20. Abidjan. ISSN-L 2708-390X, eISSN 2709-2836.
tone_statements.quote: Nos études antérieures nous ont permis d’arriver à la conclusion que la langue tagbana est une langue à tons. Cette langue compte précisément trois tons ponctuels (haut, moyen et bas) et deux tons modulés (bas haut ou montant et haut bas ou descendant). Le formalisme de chacun des tons susmentionnés se présente comme suit : • Ton haut [ ´ ]: έ, é • Ton moyen [ ˉ ]: ε̄, ē • Ton bas [ `]: ὲ, è. • Ton modulé montant (bas-haut) [ ˇ ] : ε̌, ě • Ton modulé descendant (haut-bas) [ ˆ ] : ε̂, ê
tone_statements.translation: Our earlier studies led us to the conclusion that Tagbana is a tone language. The language has precisely three level tones (high, mid and low) and two contour tones (low-high or rising and high-low or falling). The notation of each of these tones is as follows: High tone [´]: ɛ́, é; Mid tone [ˉ]: ɛ̄, ē; Low tone [`]: ɛ̀, è; Rising contour tone (low-high) [ˇ]: ɛ̌, ě; Falling contour tone (high-low) [ˆ]: ɛ̂, ê.
tone_statements.summary: 3 level + 2 contour tones; Praat F0/duration on 36 isolated, mostly monosyllabic words (mean F0 H 142, M 113, L 68 Hz). p. 18 derives the contours from crossing of H and L level tones.

tone_statements.citation: Coulibaly, Mamadou Gninnatcha Eugène. 2023. Similitudes funcionales entre acento y tonos en lenguas acentuales y tonales como español y taguana. Langues & Cultures (Université Ahmed Draia, Adrar; ASJP) 4(2): 224–243 (31 déc. 2023). ISSN 2716-8212. [in Spanish]
tone_statements.quote: La lengua taguana se identifica como lengua de tonos de registros. ... Ouattara Eugénie (2018) y Danielle Kanga (2009) están de acuerdo en que la lengua taguana consta de tres fonemas suprasegmentales que son: Tono alto [ ´ ]: ɛ́, é Tono medio [ ˉ ]: ɛ̄, ē Tono bajo [ `]: ɛ̀, è. Fuera de estos tonos, existen en la lengua taguana los tonos modulados ascendentes y descendentes. ... Los tonos modulados son antes que nada la unión de al menos dos tonos de registros. Estas uniones pueden realizarse para los tonos ascendentes mediante los tonos bajo-alto, bajo-medio, medio-alto y alto-bajo-alto. Y para los tonos descendentes, se realizan de tonos alto-bajo, medio-bajo y bajo-alto-bajo.
tone_statements.translation: Taguana is identified as a register-tone language. ... Ouattara Eugénie (2018) and Danielle Kanga (2009) agree that Taguana has three suprasegmental phonemes: high tone: ɛ́, é; mid tone: ɛ̄, ē; low tone: ɛ̀, è. Beyond these tones, Taguana has rising and falling modulated tones. ... The modulated tones are above all the union of at least two register tones. These unions are realised, for the rising tones, as low-high, low-mid, mid-high and high-low-high; and for the falling tones as high-low, mid-low and low-high-low.
tone_statements.locator: p. 228, sec. 2.2 'Descripción tonal de la lengua taguana'
tone_statements.summary: Register-tone language: high, mid, low (count credited to Ouattara 2018, Kanga 2009, adopted); contours = level sequences, though author also says 'ten suprasegmental phonemes'; syllables bear tone.
